rv.q: But as completed by Mr. Lynn, “The Emporium” doesn’t add much to Wilder’s theatrical legacy.
That spirit of danger is exactly what’s missing in this lugubrious Emporium.
The Emporium is a can't miss production, for many reasons.

Against considerable odds, The Emporium emerges as a living, breathing piece of theater—funny, strange, touching, intellectually adventurous, and finally quite overwhelming in its generosity of spirit.
The more metaphysical concerns are leavened by a committed cast, and the humor is broad but not winking.
It’s perfect for fans of Thornton Wilder to finally see the play he never finished.
Unfortunately, the metaphor overtakes the play, and it is hard to be moved by the cosmic lessons the characters learn at the end.
But while the play is distinctly Wilderian in its style and themes, it comes across today like a rambling, disjointed mess that only periodically sparks to life.

But for all their good intentions – and the excellent acting on stage – I suspect much of CSC's audience might have preferred that the pages of this extremely enigmatic play had stayed in the boxes they were found in at Yale University.

Lynn and director Rob Melrose do deserve praise for their attempt to make sense of a play that even its own author couldn’t figure out, but what we get in the end is less an emporium and more an old curiosity shop.
The show that follows throat-clearing is a mixed bag.
The answer to the last question is unfortunately more yes than no.
That you might end up with tears in your eyes is a testament to Wilder’s genius and to Lynn’s labors.

cn.t: Wilder's unfinished play, completed by Kirk Lynn, receives mixed reviews as an intriguing literary curiosity that never fully coheres. Critics praise the ambitious excavation but question whether this fragmentary work merited completion.
